 “Heart of the Beast” is a gripping survival story
 Published 12:00 pm Tuesday, November 10, 2026
 By Evan Fitch 
 Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... 
 This week at the Tryon Theatre is “Heart of the Beast” (Ayer), a heartfelt, thrilling film that explores the timeless connection between man and dog as they work together to endure the northern elements. The film has received widespread praise for its accessible entertainment, the authenticity of its central bond, and the fact that the dog doesn’t die.  
 Brad Pitt leads this film’s sparse cast as James Belmont, a special forces veteran whose service found him indebted to and enamored of a fellow warrior: a combat dog named Odin. The film follows the mutually traumatized pair as they attempt an Alaskan excursion that soon plunges them back into chaos, with their survival once again depending on each other. Pitt delivers a reliably tremendous performance opposite his wordless scene partner, but his canine compatriot matches him in effectiveness, with expressive eyes that will capture the hearts of all attendees.  
 While this film is not based on a true story, it does commit to a sincere realism in its depiction of the Special Forces world from which James and Odin hail, a world that leaves permanent scars on both. The film’s production worked diligently to ensure its “authenticity” despite the fictional narrative, keeping it grounded and gritty, with that realism heightening the intensity of its frequent thrills.  
 The film is best enjoyed without knowing the specifics of the duo’s obstacles, allowing viewers to experience the surprise of their arrival and appreciate the ingenuity and tenacity with which James and Odin overcome them. At the film’s opening, James and Odin set off in a bush plane to enjoy a relaxing period of natural isolation. Tragically, in a turn of terrible luck, they are almost immediately stranded, suffering a plane crash, and leaving them to return over 50 miles to civilization on foot, injuries and compromised supplies burdening them out of the gate.  
 “Heart of the Beast” is intense and gripping, the peril of the Alaskan wilderness keeping adrenaline flowing and pulses pounding until it brings a resounding close to its tight runtime. That said, the film’s weight comes from nature’s unrelenting peril, not from any darker element imposed by fellow man. This nuance makes the film’s intensity more palatable to younger or more sensitive audiences: danger without cruelty. However, while its thrills are frequent and effective, the film’s greatest strength lies in its heart: the emotional connection between James and Odin.  
 The purity of love mutually expressed between a human and their dog is a universally understood concept, an inseparable part of human history, and is beautifully realized in the film’s central relationship. Audiences will undoubtedly be moved to tears by the mutual dedication of these two brothers-in-arms, their protection of one another a movingly reciprocal and genuine expression of love. We hope you all will join us for the rewarding and powerful thrill ride of “Heart of the Beast”!
